dva-avc-201.text: A team wants to set up DOIS different types of logging for the stage of a API REST of the API Gateway: (1) Logs DETALHADOS showing each step of the requisition processing — result of the invocation of the authorizer, requisition/response of integration payloads, template mapping transformations and errors in each step, to DEPURATION PROFUNDA during development; and (2) a log format ESTRUTURADO AND CUSTOMS.: JSON with specific fields such as requestId, ip, caller, requestTime, httpMethod, resourcePath, status, responseLength) for ANALYTICS/business reports, sent to a separate log group for ingestion in an BI tool. What are called these two distinct logging features, and in which they differ?
options: It's the EXECUTION LOGS (CloudWatch Logs) and ACCESS LOGS. Execution logs (enabled in 'CloudWatch Stage settings, with log level INFO or ERROR) capture internal processing DETALHADO of each request — results of the authorizer, integration request/response, mapping templates and errors — aimed at DEPURATION (with considerable log volume, usually not recommended in high traffic production). FORMATO OF LOG CUSTOMIZADO (a template JSON or another, specifying exactly which fields to include, e.g.: $context.requestId, $context.identity.sourceIp) and a group of log from CloudWatch Logs Kinesis Date Firehose) of destination, directed to ANALYTICS/audit with a structured and controlled format.
Enable AWS X-Ray in the stage covers both requirements — the X-Ray provides both the internal processing details of the request and a customizable structured format for export to BI tools.
Use CloudWatch Logs Subscription Filters in the default log group of API Gateway, to separate real-time debug events from audit events in two different destinations.
They are both called 'Access Logs', differentiated only by the level of log (INFO vs ERROR) configured in the stage.
dva-avc-201.explanation: Correct. Execution logs and access logs are two sections of logging configuration INDEPENDENTES in the course of API Gateway. Execution logs provide internal processing pipeline detailing (authorizer, integration, mapping templates, errors) with level INFO/ERROR — ideal for debugging, but verbose. Access logs allow you to define a FORMATO CUSTOMIZADO (list of variables $context.*) sent to a destination of its own, ideal for structured analysis/BI, without the volume and internal detail of execution logs.
dva-avc-201.hint: Think about what are the two logging configuration sections INDEPENDENTES available for an internship of the API Gateway, and which one allows you to set a custom field format.
optionRationales: Correct. Execution logs and access logs are two sections of logging configuration INDEPENDENTES in the course of API Gateway. Execution logs provide internal processing pipeline detailing (authorizer, integration, mapping templates, errors) with level INFO/ERROR — ideal for debugging, but verbose. Access logs allow you to define a FORMATO CUSTOMIZADO (list of variables $context.*) sent to a destination of its own, ideal for structured analysis/BI, without the volume and internal detail of execution logs.

Incorrect. Execution logs and access logs are DUAS FUNCIONALIDADES DIFERENTES, set up in separate sections of the stage, each one capable independently. (INFO/ERROR) applies to EXECUTION LOGS — access logs do not have this concept of 'level', but rather a FORMATO CUSTOMIZADO Fields.

Incorrect. X-Ray provides TRACING DISTRIBUTED (times/segments), not log type DETALHADO OF PROCESSAMENTO REQUIREMENT (authorizer decisions, mapping template results) that execution logs provide, nor a CUSTOMIZEABLE structured log format with specific business fields for export to BI — that's what access logs offer.

Incorrect. API Gateway does not record a single 'combined standard log group' containing both types of information that can be divided later via subscription filters; execution logs and access logs are DUAS FUNCIONALIDADES SEPARADAS AND CONFIGURABLES INDEPENDENTEMENTE, with different contents and formats from the origin — not a single stream to be divided later.

dva-avc-202.text: The implementation of a STANDARD WORKFLOW (state machine) AWS Step Functions shows status 'FAILED' on the console. The state machine has 8 states, including parallel branches, Choice states and various Task states of Lambda with Retry/Catch settings. The team needs to quickly identify EXATAMENTE QUAL ESTADO failed, o ERRO SPECIFIC (type of exception and message) that caused the failure, and if there were attempts of Retry before the final failure — SEM scan for bones CloudWatch Logs of each function Lambda Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Check CloudWatch Logs for each function Lambda referenced in the state machine, in the order in which they appear in the flow, until you find one that recorded an error.
Enable AWS X-Ray in the state machine, because the Step Functions does not provide any native execution history mechanism — all state/error detail comes exclusively from X-Ray.

Open execution FALHA in the console of Step Functions and use the EXECUTION HISTORY / GRAPHIC VISUALIZATION OF THE FLUXO — the console stands out in red the ESTADO QUE FALHOU in the visual graph, and the Execution Event History (a chronological list of events: 'TaskStateEntered', 'TaskScheduled', 'TaskFailed', 'TaskStateExited' for the failed state, etc.) shows the exact name/cause of the error from the failed task output, including possible 'TaskFailed' attempts to RETRY before the final failure.
Use AWS CloudTrail to consult the events 'StartExecution' and 'DescriptionExecution' of the execution, which record the status and error of each step of the workflow.
dva-avc-202.explanation: Correct. Step Functions natively maintains a EXECUTION HISTORY detailed for each execution, including chronological input/output events of each state, schedule and result of each task, and error/retry events. The visual console highlights the state that has failed directly in the graph, and the Event History Execution exposes the type/message of error and the history of Retry attempts — all of this directly in the console of the Step Functions, no need to navigate the log groups of each function Lambda.
dva-avc-202.hint: Think of where the Step Functions natively records the chronological sequence of events of an execution, including entries/exit and errors of each state.
optionRationales: Correct. Step Functions natively maintains a EXECUTION HISTORY detailed for each execution, including chronological input/output events of each state, schedule and result of each task, and error/retry events. The visual console highlights the state that has failed directly in the graph, and the Event History Execution exposes the type/message of error and the history of Retry attempts — all of this directly in the console of the Step Functions, no need to navigate the log groups of each function Lambda.

Incorrect. Step Functions POSSUI an Execution History NATIVO and integrated, which shows state transitions and errors SEM X-Ray requires. X-Ray adds tracking/time visualization as a COMPLEMENTO, But it's not REQUERIDO for the basic debugging of states/errors requested in the scenario.

Incorrect. This is exactly the manual search, function by function, which the requirement explicitly asks for EVITAR; the Execution History of Step Functions aggregates this information directly, without need to verify the logs of each function individually.

Incorrect. CloudTrail register EVENTOS OF GERENCIAMENTO at the level of API (who called StartExecution, when, etc.) for the purpose of AUDITORIA, not DETALHES ESTADO-A-ESTADO execution (which state executed, your input/output, errors) within a workflow execution — this level of detail is in the Execution History of Step Functions, not in CloudTrail.

dva-avc-203.text: After implementing a new version of a microservice, a team wants to find quickly, among thousands of traces of the last 30 minutes, APENAS the traces that (a) resulted in FALHA OF SERVIDOR (5xx, 'fault' in X-Ray terminology) OR (b) had greater total response time than 2 Seconds — to investigate whether the new deployment has introduced regressions. SEM write custom code, using the X-Ray console directly. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to consult the status code application logs >= 500 OR duration > 2000, since X-Ray does not support combining multiple conditions in a single query.
Open the Service Map and manually click on each node with error indication (red) to open your individual tracks, repeating for us with high latency (yellow)).

On the X-Ray console (Traces page), use one FILTER EXPRESSION combining 'fault' and 'responsetime' — for example, 'fault = true OR responsetime > 2' — X-Ray's filter expressions syntax supports Boolean operators (AND/OR) and embedded fields (fault, error, responsetime, http.status, annotations etc.) to filter the track list interactively; the team can also SALVAR this filter expression as a X-RAY GROUP for continuous monitoring (e.g. a metric/warning of the CloudWatch based on the group trace count).
Create two separate Sampling Rules on X-Ray — one for errors 5xx and other for response time > 2 — and review the traces sampled by each rule.
dva-avc-203.explanation: Correct. The X-Ray filter expressions syntax supports combining multiple embedded fields (fault, error, responsetime), http.status, annotations etc.) with Boolean operators AND/OR directly on the Console Traces page, allowing the search 'fault = true OR responsetime > 2' without custom code. This expression can also be saved as an X-Ray Group for continuous monitoring (e.g. metrics/alarms of CloudWatch based on the group trace count).
dva-avc-203.hint: Think about which X-Ray console feature allows you to combine multiple conditions with Boolean operators (AND/OR) on fields such as 'fault' and 'responsetime' in a single search.
optionRationales: Correct. The X-Ray filter expressions syntax supports combining multiple embedded fields (fault, error, responsetime), http.status, annotations etc.) with Boolean operators AND/OR directly on the Console Traces page, allowing the search 'fault = true OR responsetime > 2' without custom code. This expression can also be saved as an X-Ray Group for continuous monitoring (e.g. metrics/alarms of CloudWatch based on the group trace count).

Wrong. X-Ray SUPORTA combine multiple conditions with Boolean operators (AND/OR) in your filter expression syntax — this distractor premise is false. Redirecting to another tool (Logs Insights) is unnecessary for something that X-Ray's own console already treats natively.

Incorrect. Sampling Rules controlam QUAIS REQUIREMENTS RASTREADAS DAQUI PARA FRENTE (pro-actively for the future), not a form of FILTRAR/PESQUISAR traces already REGISTRADOS in the last 30 minutes; this does not help to investigate traces that have already occurred.

Incorrect. This would require manually clicking on potentially many nodes, one by one, and not combining the OR condition (fault OR high latency) in a single unified list of traces — a filter expression on the Traces page returns directly to the combined and filtered list of traces that meet any of the conditions.

dva-avc-204.text: Requisition count and latency of a API e-commerce follow a DIALO standard/SEMANAL This is a very important aspect of the European Union's economic and social cohesion. LIMIAR STATISTICS on 'Invocations' (e.g. 'alarming if Invocations') < 100 in 5 minutes') generator FALSOS ALARMES common during night periods of low traffic (normal), while DEIXAR PASSAR a real traffic drop during a busy working day period (e.g., drop to 500 when 2000 The team wants an alarm that takes this VARIATION into account. NORMAL POR TIME/DIA DA SEMANA, alarming only when the traffic deviates so ANORMAL expected PARA AQUELE SPECIFIC HOURARY. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Configure the original static alarm, but increase the 'Evaluation Periods' to a very high value (ex.: 288 periods of 5 minutes = 24 hours), so that normal short-term changes are smoothed out.

Use ANOMALY DETECTION of the CloudWatch on the metric 'Invocations' — or CloudWatch applies a statistical model/machine learning trained in the metric's historical data to calculate an expected 'band' (band) of values for each point over time, taking into account daily/weekly seasonality and trend; then create an alarm based on 'ANOMALY DETECTION BAND' (e.g. alarm when the metric is out of the band in M of N data points), which adjusts the threshold dynamically per hour/day of the week instead of using a single fixed value.
Use CloudWatch Contributer Insights to automatically detect when traffic is out of the expected pattern for the current time, and set up your rules to trigger alarms from CloudWatch.

Create multiple alarms with different static thresholds, one for each time band (e.g. one threshold for business hours, one for nights, one for weekends), using EventBridge Scheduler to enable/disable each alarm at the corresponding time.
dva-avc-204.explanation: Correct. CloudWatch Anomaly Detection trains a model from metric history, capturing patterns of daily/weekly seasonality and growth trend, and produces a BANDA of expected values that vary over time. An alarm based on this band only triggers when the actual value is outside the expected range. PARA AQUELE MOMENTO SPECIFIC — removing false alarms at low normal traffic times and detecting real falls even at peak times without requiring fixed thresholds per time band.
dva-avc-204.hint: Think of what resource the CloudWatch automatically calculates an expected range of values for a metric, based on its history (including daily/weekly seasonality), instead of using a single fixed threshold.
optionRationales: Correct. CloudWatch Anomaly Detection trains a model from metric history, capturing patterns of daily/weekly seasonality and growth trend, and produces a BANDA of expected values that vary over time. An alarm based on this band only triggers when the actual value is outside the expected range. PARA AQUELE MOMENTO SPECIFIC — removing false alarms at low normal traffic times and detecting real falls even at peak times without requiring fixed thresholds per time band.

Incorrect as best approach. This is theoretically possible, but extremely laborious to build and maintain (multiple alarms, scheduled enabling/disablement rules) and does not consider the TREND OF CRESCIMENTO GRADUAL over the months; the Anomaly Detection of CloudWatch provides this adaptation dynamically and automatically from the history, without manual alarm management by period.

Incorrect. Increase evaluation periods to cover 24 hours would cause the alarm to fire based on the whole day's MEDIA, losing the ability to detect an abnormal drop in TEMPO REAL/short term during business hours — this does not solve the problem of a single static threshold being inadequate for different times, only delay/dilute detection.

Incorrect. The Contributor Insights identifies the PRINCIPAIS CONTRIBUINTES for a metric (e.g. which dimensional values contribute more), not FAIXAS ESPERADAS BASEADAS IN HOURARY for the general value of a metric; it was not designed to, nor is it natively integrated to, alarms of the way the Anomaly Detection bands do.
